title: Can you structure these 16 M&A, strategy and new business case questions in two minutes each?
description: 16 M&A, strategy and new business case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes, if you remember that every one of these is a decision with alternatives: buy or build, enter or stay out, respond or hold, sell or keep, and doing nothing is always one of the options. This mixed set covers acquisitions, valuations, competitive responses, new markets and portfolio choices. Here are 16 prompts: two minutes each, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
How to use this set

Give yourself two minutes per prompt. Deal and strategy structures usually cover the market or context, the economics for the client, risks and fit, and the alternatives. The best answers add the number that would decide it: a return against a target, profit per flight, value against price. Refreshers: how to judge an acquisition and how to respond to a competitor.

1. A rival has cut prices 20% on our best-selling product. How do we respond?

Show a model structure
  • The threat: what exactly was cut, where and for how long; can they sustain it on their costs?
  • Impact on us: customers lost so far and at risk; profit at risk in each scenario.
  • Our options: match, partly match, hold or differentiate; target only customers at risk.
  • Their reaction: risk of a price war; who can last longer.

Start: impact. How many customers actually switch? Trap: matching immediately without sizing what is at risk.

2. Should a luxury hotel group launch a budget hotel brand?

Show a model structure
  • Market: size and growth of budget hotels; competitors' returns.
  • Economics: build or conversion cost, rates and occupancy; return against cost of capital.
  • Fit and risk: can we run low-cost hotels; damage to the luxury brand.
  • Cannibalisation: guests trading down from our hotels.

Start: economics per hotel. Trap: forgetting brand risk and cannibalisation.

3. Should an airline launch a co-branded credit card?

Show a model structure
  • Customer value: who would use it; points earned and redeemed.
  • Economics: what the bank pays per card and per point; cost of reward seats.
  • Partner: which bank, terms and exclusivity.
  • Risks: the brand if the bank treats customers badly; too many free seats.

Start: what the bank pays per point against what a reward seat costs us. Trap: treating it as a brand decision when it is mainly a points business.

4. Should a coffee chain sell its beans in supermarkets?

Show a model structure
  • Market: premium coffee in supermarkets; competitors and shelf space.
  • Economics: price, retailer margin, our cost; volume to pay back.
  • Cannibalisation and halo: café visits lost against new customers and awareness.
  • Brand and operations: a premium image next to discounts; roasting capacity.

Start: net profit after any café visits lost. Trap: ignoring the effect on cafés and the brand.

5. Should a regional bakery chain buy a smaller rival for $60M?

Show a model structure
  • Target on its own: profits and growth; value against the $60M price.
  • Synergies: shared bakeries, buying and overheads; new regions.
  • Risks: integration, staff and customers lost; unknown debts or contracts.
  • Alternatives: grow organically; a different target.

Start: standalone value against price. Synergies should be the bonus, not the reason. Trap: paying the seller for synergies only the buyer can deliver.

6. Should a private equity fund buy a chain of 80 gyms?

Show a model structure
  • Market: growth and competition, budget versus premium; industry churn.
  • The company: profit per gym, best versus worst; management.
  • Value creation: new sites, pricing, cost savings; exit value and buyers.
  • Deal and risks: price, debt, return against target; leases and churn in a downturn.

Start: can the fund reach its target return at this price with a sensible plan? Trap: describing the market at length without reaching the return.

7. How would you value a football club for a potential buyer?

Show a model structure
  • Revenue: media rights, match-day and commercial; which are at risk from relegation.
  • Costs and balance sheet: wages and transfers; net debt and squad value.
  • Value methods: multiples of recent club deals; cash-flow value.
  • Strategic premium: brand, stadium and land; what this buyer adds.

Start: how safe the revenue is. Trap: using one method only; club prices often differ from cash-flow values.

8. How should an electricity company respond to the growth of rooftop solar?

Show a model structure
  • Impact: lost demand and revenue; the grid is still needed at night and in winter.
  • Defend: fixed charges versus per-kWh pricing; regulation and grid fees.
  • New services: selling solar and batteries; EV charging.
  • Costs: fixed grid costs spread over less demand; surplus plants.

Start: how much revenue is at risk and how fast. Trap: only fighting solar through tariffs instead of also selling it.

9. Should an airline launch a daily London to Lagos route?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: business, visiting family and cargo; seasonality.
  • Competition: rivals' flights, prices and loyalty; their response.
  • Economics: revenue per flight against cost per flight; what the aircraft earns elsewhere.
  • Risks: currency and getting cash out of the country; slots and approvals.

Start: profit per flight against the aircraft's best alternative use. Trap: forgetting the opportunity cost of the aircraft.

10. Should a kitchen-appliance maker stop selling its toaster range?

Show a model structure
  • Profitability: margin after allocated costs; which costs would actually go.
  • Strategic role: helps sell other products; retailer relationships.
  • Outlook: growth and price pressure; can it be fixed?
  • Exit costs: stock, tooling, contracts and staff.

Start: costs that would actually disappear. Shared overheads stay when a product goes. Trap: dropping a product that only loses money after overheads it would leave behind.

11. Should a mobile operator sell its phone towers to an infrastructure fund?

Show a model structure
  • Value: price offered against value to us; use of the cash.
  • Ongoing cost: rent we pay to use the towers; escalators in the lease.
  • Control: network upgrades and access; sharing with rivals.
  • Alternatives: sell a stake; joint venture with another operator.

Start: price received against the rent we will pay for years. Trap: seeing only today's cash.

12. Should a coffee chain buy its main coffee roaster?

Show a model structure
  • Value of the roaster: its profits and other customers; price against value.
  • Benefits to us: cheaper beans, supply security, quality control.
  • Risks: losing its other customers; running a factory.
  • Alternatives: a long-term contract; a minority stake.

Start: alternatives. A long contract may give most of the benefit without buying. Trap: assuming ownership is the only way to secure supply.

13. Should a supermarket invest in vertical farms to grow salad near its stores?

Show a model structure
  • Market: demand for fresh local salad; premium shoppers will pay.
  • Economics: cost per kg against buying from growers; energy prices.
  • Capability: run farms or partner; technology risk.
  • Strategic value: less waste, fresher produce, supply security.

Start: cost per kg, especially energy. Trap: being won over by the story before checking energy costs.

14. Should an industrial group sell its slow-growing packaging division?

Show a model structure
  • Value: sale price against value of keeping it; who would pay most.
  • Fit: links to other divisions; shared customers and costs.
  • Use of proceeds: growth, debt or returning cash; returns on each.
  • Separation: costs left behind; staff and customers.

Start: value of keeping against sale price, including costs left behind. Trap: ignoring shared costs that stay with the group.

15. Should a toy brand start selling on a large online marketplace?

Show a model structure
  • Sales gained: customers we do not reach today.
  • Margin: fees, advertising and fulfilment; price pressure.
  • Channel conflict: reaction of toy shops; sales moved from our own site.
  • Brand control: fakes and unauthorised sellers; reviews.

Start: channel conflict. Our biggest retailers may cut our shelf space. Trap: counting all marketplace sales as new.

16. A drug company's best-seller loses its patent in three years. How could it fill the gap?

Show a model structure
  • Defend the drug: new formulations; its own generic version.
  • Own pipeline: speed up late-stage drugs; focus R&D.
  • Buy and partner: acquisitions and licensing.
  • Cut costs: sales force, manufacturing, overheads.

Start: size the gap by year, then what each option adds by when. Trap: listing options without timing them against the expiry.

How to score your answer: always price the do-nothing option

Take the price cut. Suppose the product brings in $50M a year at a 30% margin, so $15M of profit, and treat all costs as variable. If we match the 20% cut and keep every customer, revenue falls to $40M while costs stay at $35M: profit drops to $5M. If we hold our price and lose a quarter of our volume, revenue is $37.5M and costs $26.25M: profit is $11.25M. Holding beats matching unless we would lose two thirds of our customers.

Strong: "Matching costs us $10M of profit for certain. Holding only does worse if we lose two thirds of volume, so I'd hold the price and protect the customers most at risk with targeted offers."

Apply the same test to deals: compare buying with building, partnering, a different target and staying as you are, and ask what price would make the deal unattractive.
